claims.text: Conventionally cast AlCoCrFeNi-type eutectic high-entropy alloys can have a dual-phase lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure.
The initial as-cast eutectic alloy exhibits the typical strength–ductility trade-off.
A short-duration treatment marginally above the eutectic solidification range can function as an annealing treatment.
The proposed treatment will refine the interlamellar spacing relative to the as-cast state.
The proposed treatment will improve phase connectivity and produce a more uniformly distributed microstructure.
The proposed treatment will reduce residual stresses.
Limited atomic diffusion during the treatment relaxes residual stresses while refining the eutectic lamellar architecture.
Finer lamellar spacing creates stronger barriers to dislocation motion and therefore increases strength.
Improved phase connectivity promotes strain accommodation between the ductile and brittle phases and therefore increases ductility.
The eutectic architecture combines a relatively soft fcc phase with a relatively hard ordered bcc/B2 phase.
Annealed samples will have statistically significantly higher yield strength than as-cast samples.
Annealed samples will have statistically significantly greater tensile elongation at failure than as-cast samples.
The relevant as-cast baseline has a coarse or otherwise non-optimized lamellar structure.
The expected improvement is intended to hold under room-temperature tensile loading.
Alloy composition, treatment temperature, and treatment duration may affect the magnitude of the microstructural and mechanical changes.
The exact strength and ductility improvements are uncertain.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in both yield strength and ductility, or failure to observe the proposed microstructural refinement, is designated as a falsifying result.

contradictions.description: The intervention is specified as occurring above the eutectic solidification range, while the mediator and mechanism describe limited solid-state diffusion, residual-stress relaxation, and subtle refinement of a retained lamellar architecture. These descriptions are internally difficult to reconcile because treatment above the solidification range implies at least partial melting rather than ordinary annealing of an intact solid microstructure.
